transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Carlos Ruiz (Redwood); Priya Nair, Samir Patel, Alina Gomez (Horizon Logistics)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Reviewed latest scorecard; drift observed on routing prompts and invoice-extraction intents.
- Two regressions flagged after model switch: increase in false positives on 'delivery exception' and a decline in recall for 'address-normalization' cases.
- Discussed guardrail tuning, prompt re-phrasing, and suggestion to pin a lighter quantized variant for low-latency routes.
- Next steps: share rubric, run micro-benchmarks, add edge-case prompts.

Topics: quality review, regression hunt, prompt set curation, scoring thresholds, guardrail config, performance tradeoffs

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everybody thanks for joining, um we'll give folks a minute but i think we have all the core people.
[00:06] Priya Nair: yeah i'm here, sorry ran a couple minutes late, my calendar overlap.
[00:08] Carlos Ruiz: all good, we can start with a quick recap, high level - we saw a few regressions after the january model swap, right?
[00:15] Alina Gomez: correct, especially on the invoice parsing flows and then an odd uptick on delivery-exception mislabels.
[00:20] Samir Patel: just to be clear, you mean the output labeling the message as an exception when it was normal delivery? we had users reporting false delivery flags.
[00:27] Priya Nair: yeah, exactly. precision dropped from 0.94 to 0.86 on that intent in the last two weeks, our team noticed.
[00:34] Maya Chen: okay that's consistent with what we saw on the scorecard -- the overall F1 stayed stable but per-intent metrics diverged. can i share my screen to show the heatmap?
[00:41] Samir Patel: go for it.
[00:43] [00:43] Carlos Ruiz: (screen share) so this is the weekly heatmap, darker red is more failures - you'll see delivery-exception and address-normalization are the two hotspots. the left column is last week's baseline, the right is current.
[00:55] Priya Nair: mhm, i see the spike. is that coming from prompt drift, or maybe the new tokenization from the updated tokenizer?
[01:03] Carlos Ruiz: it's hard to say definitively, but we did note changes in the prompt templates you shipped last week - small wording changes to the 'confirm address' scaffold which can push the model into a different parsing path.
[01:12] Alina Gomez: the product team did tweak the template to be shorter, to speed up time-to-first-token. maybe we over-optimized.
[01:18] Maya Chen: right, that's a classic latency vs quality tradeoff. we can either re-expand the prompt to include more explicit delimiters, or use guardrail rules to force extraction fallback.
[01:28] Priya Nair: what guardrail options do we have that won't add too much latency? i remember you mentioned prefix caching and some lightweight regex fallbacks?
[01:36] Carlos Ruiz: yeah. quick options: 1) an extraction-level regex fallback run inline, which is very low latency for structured fields; 2) a post-score threshold check where results below x confidence hit the deterministic parser; 3) pin a quantized smaller model variant for the route that handles short invoice snippets.
[01:50] Samir Patel: regex fallback is attractive but i'm worried about coverage, we have a lot of international address formats.
[01:56] Priya Nair: agree, regex won't catch everything, but a hybrid approach might work. run model extraction first, if low confidence or checksum mismatch then try deterministic.
[02:06] Maya Chen: exactly. also from the pilot data you shared we instrumented a checksum on postal code parse — that flagged a 12% mismatch rate on the failing cohort.
[02:15] Alina Gomez: wow 12% is higher than i expected. that explains the user reports.
[02:18] Carlos Ruiz: digging into utterances, a lot of the failures are because the prompt no longer contains the 'address markers' that used to be in the old scaffold - they removed the 'ADDRESS:' label.
[02:28] Priya Nair: oh, that was our change. we removed it to save characters.
[02:31] Maya Chen: that's a useful find. easiest path: restore a minimal explicit label like 'ADDRESS:' but keep the rest short. that often realigns the model.
[02:40] Samir Patel: can you quantify the expected quality lift from that change? a rough ballpark is fine.
[02:45] Carlos Ruiz: based on our internal A/B with similar examples, adding an ADDRESS label recovered about 6-8 percentage points in recall for normalization tasks. so you'd expect precision/recall closer to previous baseline.
[02:56] Priya Nair: ok that might be the fastest win. can we do that on the canary route and monitor?
[03:01] Maya Chen: yes, we can push a prompt tweak to the canary and watch the per-intent delta in the console. we'll set a short window, 24-48 hours, and if guardrail triggers drop we'll roll back.
[03:10] Alina Gomez: good. the other regression was on 'delivery exception' - any hypothesis there?
[03:15] Carlos Ruiz: two hypotheses: 1) model change increased tendency to hallucinate 'exception' when certain keywords appear (e.g., "delay", "hold"); 2) prompt truncation removed the customer context window so model guessed exception status.
[03:26] Maya Chen: we also noticed more false positives when emails included sentence fragments like 'holding for pickup', the model interprets as exception even if it's a scheduled status.
[03:33] Priya Nair: hmm okay. is there a simple scoring threshold we can tune to reduce false positives without sacrificing recall?
[03:38] Carlos Ruiz: yes, we can raise the decision threshold for the exception intent from 0.45 to 0.55 which historically reduced false positives by ~40% but it did drop recall 6-7%. it's a tradeoff.
[03:49] Samir Patel: do we have a confusion matrix we can look at to see which classes bleed into exception?
[03:53] Maya Chen: (shares confusion matrix) here you can see 'status-update' and 'delivery-confirmation' are the biggest confusions. the model often mislabels 'status-update' as 'exception' in short contexts.
[04:04] Alina Gomez: could we add a post-processing rule: if exception predicted but there's a timetable token like 'ETA' or explicit date, then downgrade to status-update unless confidence > 0.8?
[04:15] Carlos Ruiz: yes that's feasible and low latency. you can encode that as a rule in the route processing step. we've done similar fallback logic for financial intents.
[04:24] Priya Nair: perfect. i'd rather try rule-based fixes first before lowering recall.
[04:28] Maya Chen: agreed. we'll prototype the rule and run it on the last 48 hours of logs to validate.
[04:33] Samir Patel: on the scoring side, i wanted to call out some weirdness in the golden set - we have some borderline labels where two annotators disagreed, could that explain some of the metric churn?
[04:43] Carlos Ruiz: absolutely. label noise can look like model regression. do you have inter-annotator agreement numbers?
[04:48] Priya Nair: we haven't computed kappa for this batch, but annotator notes show about 14 cases flagged as ambiguous.
[04:54] Maya Chen: okay let's triage those ambiguous samples into a separate 'edge-case' bucket and exclude from the main scorecard or score them with partial credit.
[05:03] Alina Gomez: how many samples would you recommend we move? we don't want to butcher the dataset size.
[05:08] Carlos Ruiz: move the clearly ambiguous ones, 14 is small; also add 200 more hard negatives to make the thresholds more robust.
[05:15] Priya Nair: we can do that, we'll ask labeling to produce 200 edge cases and flag them.
[05:20] Maya Chen: great. on the ops side, i ran a micro-benchmark for latency & cost with: hosted baseline vs dedicated pinned 8-bit quantized model, batch sizes 1, 4, 8.
[05:30] Samir Patel: results?
[05:31] Carlos Ruiz: batch=1 hosted median latency ~220ms per request, dedicated quantized down to ~120ms but CPU overhead for batching bumps tail latencies if you hold for 50ms to batch. cost per 1k tokens drops ~30% on dedicated quantized path.
[05:45] Priya Nair: that's interesting. we care about p95 more than median - canyon spikes cause user-facing delays.
[05:51] Carlos Ruiz: p95 on dedicated with small batching (50ms) was 380ms, hosted p95 was ~500ms. so dedicated helps p95 too in this configuration.
[05:59] Alina Gomez: are there any quality differences between the quantized variant and the full float model? we saw a small drop in some token-level extraction.
[06:06] Carlos Ruiz: yes we observed a small delta in entity splitting accuracy - about a 1.8% drop on address tokenization in the quantized run for longer contexts, but for short invoice fields it was negligible.
[06:17] Maya Chen: so tradeoffs: dedicated quantized gives latency and cost benefits, small extraction hit on long contexts. suggestion: route short structured snippets to quantized dedicated variant and longer full-fidelity requests to hosted or unquantized dedicated.
[06:31] Priya Nair: that routing logic might be ideal. do we support dynamic routing by token-length out of the box?
[06:36] Carlos Ruiz: yes, Redwood can route by request metadata or detected length, and you can set fallback policies. we'll show a config snippet.
[06:42] Maya Chen: (uploads config link) see the example route rules. you can add a route: if tokens < 256 -> quantized-dedicated; else -> full-precision-hosted.
[06:51] Samir Patel: nice. can we get telemetry separated per-route so we can analyze regressions independently?
[06:56] Carlos Ruiz: yes, the console gives per-route breakdowns, per-model and per-prompt template. we'll enable additional tracing for the canary.
[07:04] Priya Nair: on prompt sets - we wanted your recommendation on selecting the golden prompts. our current set is 1,200 examples mostly from production but maybe skewed.
[07:14] Maya Chen: golden set should be representative across intents, edge-cases, and international formats. try stratified sampling across customers, keep a stable holdout for regression detection, and have a smaller 'daily test' of 200 items for quick checks.
[07:26] Alina Gomez: ok we can produce a stratified sample. do you recommend retaining ambiguous ones or moving them to edge-case bucket?
[07:33] Carlos Ruiz: move ambiguous to edge-case and keep them labeled separately. you can track 'score_excluding_edgecases' and 'score_including_edgecases' so you know the sensitivity.
[07:43] Priya Nair: makes sense.
[07:45] Maya Chen: quick note on scoring: we've seen teams use a weighted F1 where extraction fields have different importance; for you, a missing invoice-number is more critical than a mis-typed city, so weight accordingly.
[07:56] Samir Patel: good point. we'll map field-level business impact to weights and share that mapping.
[08:01] Alina Gomez: one more question on guardrails - can Redwood enforce a mandatory verifier step for high-value transactions? for example if invoice amount > $10k, require a secondary verification.
[08:12] Carlos Ruiz: yes, we support rule-based workflows that can route to human-in-the-loop or an alternate verification microservice. we can attach metadata and audit logs for those events.
[08:21] Priya Nair: audit logs are critical for us - we need retention for 12 months and export to our SIEM. does Redwood support S3 export and syslog?
[08:29] Maya Chen: yes we support export to S3 and streaming to external SIEMs; data residency rules can keep logs per-region. for Private deployments you can also keep the entire control plane in your VPC.
[08:40] Samir Patel: on that note, we're evaluating Dedicated vs Private - Dedicated looks fine but compliance might push us to Private for PII-heavy routes.
[08:49] Carlos Ruiz: totally understood. Private gives you full network isolation and-key management integrations; Dedicated is a good middle ground for capacity and cost. we can produce a comparison doc.
[08:59] Alina Gomez: please do. we'll need that for the security review next week.
[09:03] Maya Chen: noted, we'll attach the Dedicated vs Private matrix and include a checklist for compliance artifacts (SOC2 cert, encryption-at-rest details, KMS config).
[09:12] Priya Nair: back to regressions - what about running a rollback to prior model for the canary? has that been considered?
[09:18] Carlos Ruiz: possible, but rolling back may mask the underlying dataset/label issues. we prefer targeted prompt fixes + guardrails first, then rollback only if immediate user impact is unacceptable.
[09:30] Maya Chen: and if you want an emergency rollback plan we can prepare a one-click revert for the canary with monitoring alerts.
[09:36] Samir Patel: that comfort helps.
[09:38] Priya Nair: action items recap?
[09:40] Maya Chen: sure. 1) Priya to add 200 edge-case samples and flag ambiguous ones - due 2025-04-18. 2) Maya to share updated scoring rubric and golden prompt suggestion - due 2025-04-14. 3) Carlos to run micro-benchmarks (latency, p95, cost) for quantized dedicated vs hosted and share numbers - due 2025-04-17. 4) Redwood to prototype address-label tweak on canary and evaluate recall lift - we'll roll for 48 hours.
[10:09] Alina Gomez: noted. also please include the config snippet for route-based quantization and the sample rule for exception downgrade.
[10:16] Carlos Ruiz: will do, i'll paste the sample rule and the config link in the follow-up email.
[10:20] Priya Nair: one last practical: can you include a short checklist for the security review so we know what to prep next week?
[10:26] Maya Chen: yes we'll include the checklist: SOC2 report, SSO/SAML configs, KMS details, audit log export, network diagrams.
[10:33] Samir Patel: thank you.
[10:35] Maya Chen: awesome — unless there's anything else, we'll wrap.
[10:38] Priya Nair: nothing more from me, thanks everyone.
[10:40] Alina Gomez: thanks, bye.
[10:41] Samir Patel: bye.

Meeting end.
